sb_prompt: FIND OUT WHAT BOOKS THE OTHER CALLER READS FOR ENJOYMENT OR SELF-IMPROVEMENT.         DO YOU HAVE SIMILAR OR DIFFERENT INTERESTS IN BOOKS?
turns: Yeah, actually I'm reading *The Goldfinch* right now and thinking it's a bit pretentious, have you read any of those classics?
Yeah, I read *The Goldfinch* years ago and honestly, it felt like a whole lot of words for not much to say about.

Yeah, totally get that, I tried reading it once and felt the same way. It's just so much self-indulgence and I don't think it's about me being a child anymore, it's about me being a grown-up. It's like reading about myself but I didn't realize it was me until I got to the end. It's so raw and honest and I don't know if it's the best book or what but I can't stop thinking about it. What's the last book you read?
Yeah, last time it was this memoir about a guy who lost his memory, but honestly I just skimmed it and couldn't really get into the story.

That's too bad, but that sounds kind of depressing for a memoir. I usually just need something that feels real, not just a bunch of sad events. Have you ever read anything that made you actually feel like learning something?

Yeah, I guess *Atomic Habits* was my last real read, mostly just skimming the chapters on building routines because I thought it would help me stop wasting time on stuff I don't care about. But honestly, I don't think reading actually changed me much, just felt like I was wasting paper money trying to learn how to be a better person. I figure if I'm gonna get good at something, I should just practice it in real life, like wiring a breaker box, instead of reading about it. Do you ever find yourself thinking that books are just a waste of time compared to actually doing something?
I guess I see what you mean, but sometimes the real life stuff is just... too loud in your head, and reading gives me a quiet place to sort it out before I try fixing it myself.
Yeah, that actually makes sense, but I don't get that quiet place thing; I usually just feel like I'm talking to myself louder if I don't just go fix the thing.
I get that, honestly, wiring a box is just tangible proof you fixed it, whereas reading is just me sitting there trying to organize the noise in my head before I even touch the problem.
Yeah, that's a fair point, but I still think reading is just me trying to fix a wiring job with a paintbrush—like, sure it looks nice on the wall, but it doesn't make the light turn on.
That's a fair way to put it, but maybe the book isn't supposed to turn the light on, just help me understand why it burned out in the first place so I don't mess up the next job?
That's a good analogy, but I still feel like I'm reading the manual for a tool I don't need just to use the hammer I already have.

Right, maybe the book isn't the hammer but the flashlight to see where you're working in the dark. Have you read anything that actually changed the way you approached a job or fixed a specific problem?
Yeah, actually I did read *Thinking, Fast and Slow* a while back and it was kind of useful, mostly just helped me stop overthinking simple math problems before I call a client.

That's actually a really good point, because honestly, I read a bunch of financial books once when I first started doing taxes and felt exactly the same way—like I was trying to fix my brain with a hammer instead of just doing the math. But then I read this book by someone named James Clear about habits, and it changed how I look at my own work; it helped me realize that my biggest mistakes weren't about knowing the formulas, but about how I was organizing my whole day, which is weird for an accountant, but whatever. It made me stop rushing through my clients' returns and actually take a minute to think about their situation before I started typing. Does that make sense, or is it still just too much theory for you?

Yeah, that actually kind of resonates, but I still feel like I'm just memorizing a checklist instead of actually feeling smarter. I guess I'll keep trying to read the manual, but if it doesn't help me diagnose the breaker faster, I'm probably just wasting time.

Yeah, fair enough, I get the checklist thing, but maybe for me the flashlight is what lets me see the part of the blueprint that wasn't drawn right in the first place, so I don't have to go back and tear the whole thing down later.
Yeah, maybe the flashlight thing is useful if you're in the dark, but if you've got a flashlight in a room full of windows, I'm just gonna go climb up there and check the fuse anyway.

Haha, that's a fair point—maybe you don't need the flashlight if you're already standing right next to the light. I guess I'll keep reading just to make sure I don't end up blind in my own office someday.
Yeah, sure, but if you're already standing in the light, I'd rather just check the breaker and get back to work before the clients start asking questions.
Haha, good point, I guess I'll stop reading the blueprint just to check the fuse myself.
Yeah, fair enough, I'll probably just stick to the manuals and get back to work.
Haha, point taken, I'll probably just stick to the math and let you check the fuse.
Yeah, that sounds like a solid plan for you, so I'm gonna go grab my tools and see if I can finally get that outlet fixed without second-guessing myself.
Haha, yeah, good luck with the outlet, I'm off to finish this chapter before I start overthinking the whole story.
Take care, and good luck with that story.
Haha, deal, thanks for hanging out!
